tool.name: CSS
tool.tagline: The style sheet language that lays out and styles every web page
tool.description: CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls how HTML looks: colours, typography, spacing, layout, responsiveness and animation. Modern CSS has flexbox, grid, container queries, custom properties, cascade layers and nesting, so most layouts need no framework and no JavaScript. Every front-end developer, and anyone who builds web pages, needs it.

glossary.def: The part of a CSS rule that picks which elements it styles, such as h1 (every main heading) or .card (every element with the class card).
One setting inside a CSS rule, written property: value; such as color: navy;
In CSS, one setting you can change on an element, such as color, width or font-size. You give it a value in a declaration: color: navy;
A CSS instruction starting with @, such as @media or @font-face, that sets conditions or settings for other rules instead of styling elements directly.
A safe value or option used when the preferred one isn't available, such as a common font listed after a special one, or an older colour format written before a newer one.
Panels built into every browser (right-click a page and choose Inspect) that show a page's elements, the CSS applied to them, downloads, errors and speed.
In HTML and CSS, a group name given to elements with the class attribute, like class="card". CSS selects them with a dot: .card.
A symbol between two CSS selectors that picks elements by relationship: a space (anywhere inside), > (directly inside), + (right after) or ~ (any later sibling).
An element that sits inside another one, at any depth: its children, their children, and so on.
An element that has the same parent element as another one, like two list items in the same list.
An element that contains another one, at any depth: its parent, the parent's parent, and so on up to <html>.
CSS's fixed process for choosing which declaration wins when several set the same property on an element: importance, then layers, then specificity, then order.
A score for how precisely a CSS selector targets an element, counted as (ids, classes and similar, tag names). When rules clash, the higher score wins.
In CSS, some properties, mostly text ones like color and font-family, pass down from an element to the elements inside it unless they set their own value.
A colour written as # and six digits or letters, like #1e90ff: three pairs giving the amounts of red, green and blue, from 00 (none) to ff (full).
In CSS, a value written as a name with inputs in brackets, such as calc(100% - 2rem), rgb(0 0 0) or rotate(45deg).
A CSS length unit equal to the font size of the page's <html> element: 16px by default, and larger if the reader raises their browser's text size.
The part of the browser window that shows the page. On a phone it's the whole screen apart from the browser's own bars.
The way CSS sees every element: a rectangle made of the content, then padding, then a border, then a margin outside.
In CSS, the space between an element's content and its border. It shows the element's background colour.
In CSS, the empty space outside an element's border that keeps neighbouring elements away.
CSS properties named after the direction of text rather than the screen, like margin-inline-start instead of margin-left, so layouts flip correctly for right-to-left languages.
A CSS rule where the top and bottom margins of blocks that meet merge into one gap the size of the larger margin, instead of adding up.
How a browser arranges elements when no layout CSS is applied: blocks stack from top to bottom, and inline content runs along in lines of text.
In CSS, an element that arranges or measures the elements inside it, such as a flex or grid container, or an element marked for container queries.
A list of fonts in font-family. The browser uses the first one it has, so the list ends with a general family like sans-serif that always exists.
A font file the browser downloads with the page, declared with @font-face, so text looks the same even if the reader doesn't have that font installed.
A single font file that holds a whole range of weights (and sometimes widths), instead of one file per weight.
In CSS, a smooth blend from one colour to another, used as a background image, such as linear-gradient(to right, blue, pink).
The CSS layout set on with display: flex. It lines up the elements inside in one direction, side by side or stacked, and shares out the space between them.
An element with display: flex. It arranges the elements directly inside it, its flex items, in a row or a column.
An element directly inside a flex container, which the container sizes and lines up.
In flexbox, the direction the items are lined up in: across for flex-direction: row, downwards for column. justify-content works along it.
In flexbox, the direction at right angles to the main axis: downwards for a row, across for a column. align-items works along it.
A selector part starting with one colon that matches elements in a state or position, such as :hover (the mouse is over it) or :first-child.
A selector part starting with two colons that styles one part of an element, or adds a decorative box, such as ::first-line or ::before.
The element, such as a link, button or text field, that keyboard input currently goes to. Pressing Tab moves it to the next one.
The box that a positioned element's top, right, bottom and left are measured from, usually its nearest ancestor that has a position other than static.
The CSS layout set on with display: grid. It places the elements inside into rows and columns at the same time.
One row or one column of a CSS grid.
A CSS grid unit meaning one share of the leftover space: two columns of 1fr and 2fr split it one third to two thirds.
A CSS value you name yourself, starting with --, such as --brand: navy; and read anywhere with var(--brand).
One named value of a design system, such as a brand colour, a spacing step or a corner radius, defined once (often as a custom property) and reused everywhere.
A CSS block, written @media (condition) { ... }, whose rules apply only when the condition is true, such as a minimum screen width or dark mode being on.
Building one web page that adapts its layout to any screen size, from phone to wide desktop monitor.
In CSS, a screen or container width at which the layout changes, set with a media or container query.
Writing the CSS for small screens first, as the base, then adding media queries that adjust the layout as more space becomes available.
In CSS, a smooth change of a property from its old value to its new one over a set time, instead of an instant jump.
A CSS animation described as a sequence of steps (from, to, or percentages), which runs on its own once applied with the animation property.
How an animation's speed changes over its duration, such as linear (steady) or ease (slow start, faster middle, slow end).
A CSS effect that moves, turns, resizes or slants how an element is drawn, without changing the space it takes up in the layout.
Writing CSS rules inside other rules, so the inner selector applies relative to the outer one, with & standing for the outer selector.
A CSS block, written @container (condition) { ... }, whose rules apply depending on the size of an ancestor element rather than the whole screen.
A named group of CSS rules, created with @layer. A later layer beats an earlier one however specific its selectors are.
A tiny CSS class that does one job, such as .mb-0 for margin-bottom: 0, combined in the HTML to style elements.
A team's shared set of design rules, values and ready-made components, so every page looks and behaves consistently.
A group of elements that is layered as a unit: z-index only orders elements within the same group, and the whole group sits at one level in its parent group.
A CSS property that decides which of several overlapping positioned elements is drawn on top; higher numbers are closer to the viewer.
Block, Element, Modifier: a naming style for CSS classes, such as .card, .card__title and .card--featured, so every selector is a single class.
Limiting CSS so it applies only inside one component or part of the page, instead of to the whole site.
An area of the page where blocks are stacked by one set of rules; margins don't collapse across its edge, and it keeps floated children inside.
An older CSS feature (float: left or right) that moves a box to one side so the following text wraps around it, like a photo in a magazine.
Slowness caused by a script that keeps changing styles and then reading sizes, forcing the browser to recalculate the layout over and over.
A system for describing colours with numbers, such as sRGB (used by hex and rgb()) or oklch.
The standard range of colours that ordinary screens have shown for decades, and that hex, rgb() and hsl() colours describe.
The range of colours a screen can show. Many newer screens have a wide gamut: more vivid colours than standard sRGB.
Describes colour numbers that match how eyes see: two colours with the same lightness value look equally light, which is true of oklch but not of hsl.
A size a box gets from its own content, such as the width of its longest word or of its text with no wrapping.
The narrowest a box can be without its content spilling out: roughly the width of its longest word or widest image.
The width a box would have if none of its text wrapped onto a new line.

concepts.name: Rules, declarations and linking CSS
concepts.summary: A CSS rule is a selector plus declarations; attach styles with a linked stylesheet, a style element or an inline style.
concepts.why: Everything in CSS is written as rules, so reading and placing them correctly comes first.
concepts.body:
HTML says what is on a page; CSS says how it looks. You write CSS as a list of instructions such as "make every main heading navy and large". A file or block of these instructions is called a **stylesheet**. Each instruction is a **rule**. A rule starts with a **selector**, which picks the elements it applies to: `h1` picks every `

` on the page. After the selector, inside curly braces, come the rule's **declarations**. Each one names a **property** (one setting you can change, such as `color` or `font-size`), then a colon, a value and a semicolon: ```css h1 { color: navy; font-size: 2rem; } ``` There are three places to put CSS: - **External stylesheet**: a separate `.css` file, connected with `` in the head. This is the normal choice. Every page shares the one file, and the browser keeps a saved copy, so moving to the next page doesn't download it again. - **Style element**: `` in the head, handy for small demos and one-page experiments. - **Inline style**: `

`. It applies to one element only and beats almost every rule in a stylesheet, which makes it hard to change later. Avoid it, except for values that JavaScript sets. Browsers are forgiving. A declaration with a misspelled property, or a value the browser doesn't understand, is silently **dropped**, and the rest of the rule still applies. That lets you write a **fallback**: put an older, widely supported value first and a newer one after it. Browsers that understand the newer value use it; others keep the older one. The downside is that typos fail without any error message. Right-click the page and choose Inspect to open the browser's **developer tools**: the Styles panel shows dropped declarations struck through, with a warning icon. Comments are written `/* ... */`; CSS has no `//` comments. Rules that start with `@`, such as `@media` and `@font-face`, are called **at-rules**. Instead of styling elements directly, they set conditions or settings for other rules; later lessons cover the common ones.
takeaways: A rule = selector + { property: value; } declarations
Prefer external stylesheets; avoid inline styles
Invalid declarations are dropped silently: check developer tools
pitfalls: Writing // comments, which break the following rule.

quiz.q: A rule contains 'color: blu; font-weight: bold;'. What happens?
options: The page fails to load the stylesheet
The color declaration is dropped, bold still applies
The color falls back to blue
quiz.explain: Only the invalid declaration is discarded; valid ones in the same rule still apply.

concepts.name: Selectors and combinators
concepts.summary: Target elements by tag name, class, id and attribute, and by where they sit inside other elements, using combinators.
concepts.why: Precise selectors are how you style exactly the elements you mean and nothing else.
concepts.body:
A selector chooses which elements a rule applies to. There are a few simple kinds:

- type: `p`, `button` (every element with that tag name)
- class: `.card` matches any element with `class="card"`. Remember from HTML that an element can have several classes, separated by spaces.
- id: `#main` matches the one element with `id="main"`. Avoid ids for styling: they win too easily over other rules, as the next lesson shows.
- attribute: `[disabled]`, `[type="email"]`, `[href^="https"]` (value starts with), `[href$=".pdf"]` (value ends with)
- universal: `*` matches every element

Write them together with no space to require all at once: `button.primary[disabled]` is a disabled button that also has the class `primary`.

Elements sit inside each other like folders. An element directly inside another is its **child**, and the outer one is its **parent**. Elements inside at any depth are **descendants**; elements that share a parent are **siblings**.

**Combinators** are the symbols between selectors that select by these relationships:

- `nav a` (a space): an `a` anywhere inside a `nav`.
- `ul > li`: an `li` whose parent is a `ul`.
- `h2 + p`: the `p` that comes right after an `h2`, with the same parent.
- `h2 ~ p`: every `p` that comes after an `h2`, with the same parent.

A comma makes a **selector list**: `h1, h2, h3 { ... }` applies the rule to all three.

Keep selectors short. Long chains like `main div > ul li a` break as soon as someone changes the HTML around them. Instead, give each piece of the page (a card, a menu) a class that says what it is, and select by that.
concepts.code:
/*
Home Docs
*/ .menu a { text-decoration: none; } /* descendant */ .menu > a { padding: 4px 8px; } /* direct child */ a[href$=".pdf"]::after { content: " (PDF)"; } /* attribute: ends with */ h2 + p { margin-top: 0; } /* first p right after an h2 */ input[type="checkbox"] { accent-color: teal; } button.primary { background: royalblue; color: white; } /* both at once */ button .icon { width: 1em; } /* .icon INSIDE a button */
takeaways: Class selectors are the workhorse; avoid ids for styling
space = descendant, > = child, + = next sibling, ~ = later siblings
No space means 'same element': a.b is different from a .b
pitfalls: Writing 'button .primary' (descendant) when you meant 'button.primary' (same element).

quiz.q:
Which elements does 'ul > li' match in
  • A
    1. B
?
quiz.explain: > requires a direct parent ul; B's parent is an ol.

concepts.name: Cascade, specificity and inheritance
concepts.summary: Learn how the browser picks a winner when several rules set the same property, and which properties pass down to the elements inside.
concepts.why: Most 'my CSS doesn't work' moments are the cascade doing exactly what it's specified to do.
concepts.body:
Often two rules try to set the same property on the same element: one says a paragraph is green, another says purple. The browser needs a fixed way to pick the winner. Its set of rules for this is the **cascade**, the "C" in CSS. It checks, in order:

- **Origin and importance**: browsers have a built-in stylesheet (that's why links start out blue and underlined), and your styles beat it. Writing `!important` after a value makes that declaration beat normal ones.
- **Cascade layers** (`@layer`): covered in an advanced lesson.
- **Specificity**: the more specific selector wins.
- **Order**: if everything else is equal, the declaration that comes last wins.

**Specificity** is a score of three numbers (A, B, C). A counts ids. B counts classes, attribute selectors and pseudo-classes such as `:hover` (a later lesson). C counts type selectors like `p`. `#nav .link` scores (1,1,0) and beats `.menu .link:hover` at (0,3,0), because one id outranks any number of classes. An inline `style` attribute beats any selector, and `*` and combinators add nothing.

**Inheritance** is a separate idea: some properties pass down from an element to everything inside it. Mostly these are text properties, like `color`, `font-family`, `font-size` and `line-height`: set `font-family` on `body` and every paragraph uses it. Box properties like `margin`, `border`, `width` and `background` don't pass down.

You can control this with special values. `inherit` copies the parent's value, and `initial` resets the property to its built-in default.

An inherited value always loses to any rule that targets the element itself, however weak its selector. That's why `body { color: gray }` doesn't turn links gray: the browser's built-in stylesheet has a rule for `a` itself.

Treat `!important` as a last resort. Once one rule uses it, the next fix needs it too. Keep selectors short and similar in strength instead.
concepts.code:
/*

Hello link

*/ p { color: black; } /* (0,0,1) */ .lead { color: green; } /* (0,1,0) beats p */ #intro { color: purple; } /* (1,0,0) beats .lead -> text is purple */ p.lead { color: orange; } /* (0,1,1) still loses to the id */ body { font-family: Georgia, serif; } /* inherited by p and a */ .lead { border: 1px solid; } /* NOT inherited by the link */ a { color: inherit; } /* opt in: link takes the p's purple */
takeaways: Order of checks: importance, layer, specificity, then order in the file
Specificity = (ids, classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, types)
Text properties inherit; box properties don't
A rule that targets the element always beats an inherited value
pitfalls: Reaching for !important instead of fixing specificity.

quiz.q: Which wins for color: '.card .title' (two classes) or '#hero h2' (id + type)?
options: Whichever comes last in the file
They combine into a mixed colour
'#hero h2', one id outranks any number of classes
quiz.explain: Specificity compares ids first: (1,0,1) beats (0,2,0).

concepts.name: Colours, units and values
concepts.summary: Write colours in hex, rgb, hsl and oklch, and choose between px, rem, em, %, vw and other units for sizes.
concepts.why: Picking the right unit is the difference between a layout that adapts to the reader's settings and one that breaks.
concepts.body:
**Colours** can be written several ways:

- Names: `red`, `rebeccapurple`, `transparent`, and `currentColor` (the element's own text colour).
- **Hex colours**: `#1e90ff` gives amounts of red, green and blue as three pairs of digits and letters, from `00` (none) to `ff` (full). An extra pair, as in `#1e90ff80`, sets how see-through it is.
- `rgb(30 144 255 / 50%)` gives red, green and blue from 0 to 255; the part after `/` is the opacity: how solid the colour is, from 100% (solid) down to 0% (invisible). `hsl(210 100% 56%)` gives hue (an angle around the colour wheel), saturation and lightness.
- `oklch(65% 0.2 250)` gives lightness, chroma (how vivid) and hue. Equal lightness values really look equally light to the eye, which rgb and hsl don't promise, so building a palette is easier. All current browsers support it.

Things written as a name with values in brackets, such as `rgb(...)`, are CSS **functions**.

**Lengths** come in two families.

- Absolute: `px`, the CSS pixel. On sharp phone screens one CSS pixel covers several physical dots, so sizes look about the same on every screen.
- Relative: `rem` is a multiple of the root font size (the font size of the `<html>` element: 16px unless the reader changes it). `em` is a multiple of the element's own font size, and `%` is a share of the parent's size.

The **viewport** is the visible area of the browser window. `vw` and `vh` are 1% of its width and height, and `ch` is the width of a "0" in the current font.

A good default: `rem` for font sizes and most spacing, so everything grows when a reader raises their browser's font size; `px` for borders and thin lines; `%` for widths. `em` multiplies when elements are nested, which is handy for the space inside a button but confusing for font sizes in nested lists.

On phones, `100vh` can be taller than what's visible, because of the browser's toolbars. Use `100dvh` (the visible height right now) or `100svh` (the smallest it gets) instead.

`calc()` does arithmetic and can mix units: `calc(100% - 2rem)`.
takeaways: rem for text and spacing, px for borders
oklch gives colours that look evenly spaced
Use dvh/svh instead of vh for full-height phone layouts
calc() mixes units
pitfalls: Setting font sizes in px only, or shrinking the root size with html { font-size: 62.5% }, which works against the reader's chosen text size.

quiz.q: With the default root font size, .box { font-size: 20px; padding: 2em; } has how much padding?
quiz.explain: em on padding is relative to the element's own font size: 2 x 20px.

concepts.name: The box model
concepts.summary: Every element is a box of content, padding, border and margin; box-sizing decides whether width includes padding and border.
concepts.why: Most spacing and sizing surprises come from misunderstanding how these four layers add up.
concepts.body:
The browser lays out every element as a rectangle, a **box**, with four layers from the inside out:

- **content**: the text or child elements, sized by `width` and `height`;
- **padding**: space inside the border, which shows the element's background;
- **border**: the visible edge;
- **margin**: transparent space outside the border, pushing neighbours away.

By default (`box-sizing: content-box`), `width` sets only the content. A box with `width: 300px`, `padding: 20px` and a 1px border takes up 342px: 300 + 2 × 20 + 2 × 1. Almost every project switches to `box-sizing: border-box`, where `width` includes padding and border, so the box is exactly 300px.

Margin and padding take one to four values, going clockwise from the top: `margin: 10px 20px` means 10px top and bottom, 20px left and right.

You can also use the **logical properties** `margin-block` (top and bottom) and `margin-inline` (left and right), plus `padding-inline-start` and friends. "Start" means the side text starts on, so these flip automatically for languages written right to left, such as Arabic and Hebrew.

`margin-inline: auto` centres a block that has a width: the two automatic margins share the leftover space equally.

One surprise: the top and bottom margins of block elements that sit one after another **collapse**. Two paragraphs with `margin: 20px` end up 20px apart, not 40px; only the larger margin counts. Padding never collapses, and margins don't collapse inside the flex and grid layouts of later lessons.

Open developer tools and select an element: the box-model diagram shows each layer's exact size. It's the fastest way to find out where unexpected space comes from.
takeaways: content + padding + border + margin
box-sizing: border-box makes width include padding and border
margin-inline: auto centres a block with a width
Top and bottom margins between blocks collapse to the larger one
pitfalls: Adding padding to a width: 100% element with content-box and getting a horizontal scrollbar.

quiz.q: With box-sizing: content-box, width: 200px, padding: 10px, border: 2px, what is the rendered width?
quiz.explain: 200 content + 2 x 10 padding + 2 x 2 border = 224px.

concepts.name: Display and normal flow
concepts.summary: Control how a box takes part in layout with display: block, inline, inline-block, none, and understand normal flow.
concepts.why: Normal flow is the default layout every other technique builds on or breaks out of.
concepts.body:
Without any layout CSS, elements are arranged by **normal flow**, the way the HTML lessons described: block boxes stack from top to bottom, each as wide as the space allows, and inline boxes sit side by side in lines of text and wrap like words.

The `display` property changes how a box takes part:

- `block`: starts a new line and takes the full width; `width`, `height` and top and bottom margins all work.
- `inline`: flows in the text. `width` and `height` are ignored, and top and bottom padding and margins don't push other lines away.
- `inline-block`: flows in the text like a word but can be sized like a block, which suits buttons and badges.
- `none`: removes the element completely, both from the page and from what screen readers announce.
- `flex` and `grid`: the element becomes a **container** that arranges the elements directly inside it. The next lessons cover both.

`display` really sets two things: how the box behaves next to its siblings (block or inline) and how it arranges its own children (normal flow, flex or grid). That's why `inline-flex` exists: a box that sits in a line of text and arranges its children with flex.

There are several ways to hide an element, with different effects:

- `display: none`: takes no space, isn't drawn, and screen readers skip it.
- `visibility: hidden`: invisible, but still takes up its space.
- `opacity: 0`: invisible and takes up space, yet can still be clicked and reached with the Tab key.

Sometimes you want text that is hidden on screen but still read aloud, like a label for an icon-only button. `display: none` hides it from screen readers too. Use a small reusable class, usually named `visually-hidden`, that shrinks the element to 1px and clips it; copy it from the example below.
takeaways: Normal flow: blocks stack, inline boxes wrap in lines
Inline boxes ignore width and height; inline-block doesn't
display: none removes it for everyone, screen readers included; visibility: hidden keeps the space
pitfalls: Setting width on a span and wondering why nothing changes.

quiz.q: Which hides an element but keeps its space in the layout?
quiz.explain: visibility: hidden makes the box invisible while it still occupies space.

concepts.name: Typography and web fonts
concepts.summary: Style text with font-family stacks, size, weight, line-height and spacing, and load custom fonts efficiently with @font-face.
concepts.why: Text is most of what users read; good type settings matter more for readability than any other styling.
concepts.body:
Most of a page is text, and a handful of properties control it.

- `font-family` takes a list of fonts, called a **font stack**: `"Inter", system-ui, sans-serif`. The browser uses the first font it has. The last entry should be a general family such as `sans-serif` or `serif`, which always exists.
- `system-ui` means the font your computer or phone uses for its own menus. It looks familiar and needs no download.
- `font-size` in `rem`; `font-weight` from 100 to 900 (400 is normal, 700 bold); `font-style: italic`.
- `line-height` is the height of each line of text. Write it without a unit, around 1.4 to 1.6 for body text. A number without a unit is multiplied by each element's own font size. A fixed value like `24px` is inherited as 24px everywhere, which squashes larger headings.
- `letter-spacing`, `text-transform`, `text-align`, `text-decoration`.
- `max-width: 65ch` keeps lines short enough to read comfortably.

To use a font the reader doesn't have, a **web font**, describe it with the `@font-face` at-rule: a family name, the URL of the font file and the weights it covers. Use WOFF2 files, the standard web font format, which is packed small to download faster. A **variable font** holds a whole range of weights in one file: `font-weight: 100 900`.

`font-display: swap` shows the text in a fallback font straight away, then switches to the web font once it has downloaded. Without it, browsers may hide the text for up to three seconds. Keep the font files on your own site, and stick to a couple of families and weights: each file is a separate download.

`clamp(smallest, preferred, largest)` makes sizes that grow with the screen, within limits: `font-size: clamp(1.5rem, 1rem + 2vw, 2.5rem)`. Keep a `rem` part in the middle value, so the size still responds when the reader zooms.
takeaways: Always end a font stack with a general family like sans-serif
Write line-height without a unit
WOFF2 + font-display: swap for web fonts
clamp() gives sizes that grow with the screen, within limits
pitfalls: Setting line-height in px on body, so big headings inherit a cramped fixed line height.

quiz.q: Why is line-height: 1.5 usually better than line-height: 24px on body?
options: The number is multiplied by each element's own font size
quiz.explain: Elements inside inherit the number, not a fixed length, so big text gets a proportionally taller line.

concepts.name: Backgrounds, borders and shadows
concepts.summary: Decorate boxes with background colours, images and gradients, rounded borders, outlines and shadows.
concepts.why: These are the everyday properties that turn plain boxes into buttons, cards and banners.
concepts.body: **Backgrounds** paint behind the content and padding. - `background-color`, and `background-image`, which can be a picture, `url("photo.jpg")`, or a **gradient**: a smooth blend from one colour to another, such as `linear-gradient(to right, #6366f1, #ec4899)`. There are also `radial-gradient(...)` (out from a centre) and `conic-gradient(...)` (round a centre, like a pie chart). - `background-size: cover` fills the box, cropping the image as needed; `contain` fits the whole image in. - `background-position: center` and `background-repeat: no-repeat` control placement. - You can stack several backgrounds, separated by commas; the first one is drawn on top. **Borders**: `border: 1px solid #ddd` sets width, style and colour at once. For one side, use `border-top` or the logical `border-block-start`. `border-radius` rounds the corners: `8px` for cards, `50%` for a circle (on a square box), `999px` for a pill shape. **Outline** looks like a border but takes no space and never moves anything. That's why browsers use it for the **focus outline**: the ring around the link or button that keyboard input will go to. `outline-offset` moves it out from the edge. **Shadows**: `box-shadow: 0 4px 12px rgb(0 0 0 / 15%)` takes a sideways shift, a downward shift, a blur size, an optional spread and a colour. Add `inset` for a shadow inside the box, and separate several shadows with commas for more realistic depth. `text-shadow` does the same for text, and `filter: drop-shadow()` follows the outline of images with see-through parts. Images that carry meaning belong in HTML, as `` with alt text. CSS backgrounds are for decoration only, because screen readers can't see them.
takeaways: Gradients are background images; layers are comma-separated, first on top
border-radius: 50% makes a circle
outline takes no space, which suits focus outlines
Meaningful images go in HTML, decoration in CSS
pitfalls: Removing the focus outline for looks without giving keyboard users another clearly visible focus style.

quiz.q: In background: url(a.png), url(b.png), which image is drawn on top?
options: Only the last one is used
quiz.explain: The first background layer listed is painted on top.

concepts.name: Flexbox
concepts.summary: Lay items out side by side or stacked with flexbox, sharing out space and aligning them with justify-content, align-items and gap.
concepts.why: Flexbox handles menus, toolbars, centring and rows of cards: most layouts that run in one direction.
concepts.body:
`display: flex` turns an element into a **flex container**, and the elements directly inside it into **flex items**. The items are lined up in one direction.

- `flex-direction: row` (the default) puts them side by side; `column` stacks them. The direction they're lined up in is the **main axis**; the other direction is the **cross axis**.
- `justify-content` spreads items along the main axis: `flex-start`, `center`, `space-between`, `space-around`, `space-evenly`.
- `align-items` lines them up on the cross axis: `stretch` (the default: equal heights), `center`, `flex-start`, or `baseline` (the bottoms of their first lines of text line up).
- `gap: 1rem` puts space between items without any margins.
- `flex-wrap: wrap` lets items move onto a new line instead of getting squeezed.

Each item's size is set with the `flex` property, which takes three values: `flex: grow shrink basis`. The basis is the item's starting size. Grow says how much of the leftover space it takes; shrink says how much it gives up when there isn't enough room.

- `flex: 1` means "start from nothing and take an equal share of the space".
- `flex: none` keeps the item at its content's size, neither growing nor shrinking.
- `flex: 0 0 200px` makes a fixed 200px column.

Two classic recipes: centring anything with `display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center`, and pushing one item to the far end with `margin-left: auto`, because an automatic margin soaks up all the leftover space.

Remember that `justify-content` follows the main axis, so with `flex-direction: column` it works vertically. And flexbox handles one direction at a time: when both rows *and* columns must line up, use grid (the next level).
takeaways: justify-content = main axis, align-items = cross axis
gap spaces items; flex-wrap allows new lines
flex: 1 shares the leftover space; flex: none keeps content size
margin-left: auto pushes an item to the end
pitfalls: Expecting justify-content to centre horizontally in a flex-direction: column container; there, align-items does that.

quiz.q: In a flex-direction: column container, which property centers items horizontally?
quiz.explain: With a column direction the cross axis is horizontal, and align-items works on the cross axis.

concepts.name: Pseudo-classes and pseudo-elements
concepts.summary: Style elements by state or position with pseudo-classes like :hover and :nth-child, and generate content with ::before and ::after.
concepts.why: Interactive states and structural styling are impossible without them, and they save you adding lots of extra HTML.
concepts.body:
**Pseudo-classes** start with one colon and select elements in a particular state or position, such as "the mouse is over it" or "it's the first item".

- User action: `:hover`, `:active`, `:focus`, and `:focus-visible`. An element has **focus** when keyboard input will go to it; `:focus-visible` matches only when the browser would show a focus outline (after keyboard use, not mouse clicks). Use it for focus styles.
- Form state: `:checked`, `:disabled`, `:required`, `:invalid`, `:user-invalid`, `:placeholder-shown`.
- Structure: `:first-child`, `:last-child`, `:only-child`, `:nth-child(2n+1)` (odd items), `:nth-child(3)`, `:nth-of-type()`, `:empty`.
- Negation: `:not(.active)`.
- Links: `:link` and `:visited` (for privacy, only colours can change on visited links).

**Pseudo-elements** start with two colons. They style one part of an element, or add a box that isn't in the HTML.

- `::before` and `::after` insert a generated child at the start or end. They require the `content` property, even if it's just `content: ""`, and they don't work on elements that have no end tag, like `img` and `input`.
- `::first-line`, `::first-letter`, `::placeholder`, `::selection`, `::marker` (list bullets), `::backdrop` (the layer behind a pop-up dialog that blocks the page).

Generated content is decoration. Screen readers may or may not read it, and users can't select it, so never put essential information in `content`.

A useful recipe: `li:not(:last-child)` adds separators between items without an extra one after the last.
takeaways: Pseudo-classes = state/position (:hover); pseudo-elements = parts (::before)
Use :focus-visible for focus outlines
::before/::after need a content property
Generated content is decoration, not information
pitfalls: Forgetting content: "" so ::before never appears.

quiz.q: Which selector matches the 1st, 3rd, 5th... items of a list?
quiz.explain: odd is the same as 2n+1, matching positions 1, 3, 5 and so on.

concepts.name: Positioning
concepts.summary: Take boxes out of normal flow with relative, absolute, fixed and sticky positioning and the inset properties.
concepts.why: Badges, dropdowns, sticky headers and overlays all depend on positioning and on finding the right containing block.
concepts.body:
`position` decides how `top`, `right`, `bottom`, `left` (or the shorthand `inset`) are applied.

- `static` (default): normal flow; inset properties do nothing.
- `relative`: stays in flow, but is shifted visually by the offsets. Its original space is kept. Mostly used as an anchor for absolutely positioned children.
- `absolute`: taken out of flow (siblings close the gap) and positioned relative to its **containing block**: the nearest ancestor whose position isn't static. If there's none, it uses the initial containing block: a viewport-sized area at the top of the page.
- `fixed`: positioned relative to the viewport; it stays put when the page scrolls. (A famous surprise: if an ancestor has a `transform`, from the next lesson, or a `filter`, a visual effect such as blur, that ancestor becomes the containing block instead.)
- `sticky`: behaves like relative until scrolling would move it past its offset, e.g. `top: 0`, then sticks within its parent's bounds.

The usual recipe for a badge on a card: parent `position: relative`, child `position: absolute; top: 8px; right: 8px`. `inset: 0` on an absolute child covers the parent completely, which is ideal for overlays.

When sticky doesn't stick, the cause is almost always an ancestor with `overflow: hidden` or `auto`, settings that clip or scroll content that doesn't fit (sticky then sticks inside that scrolling box), or a parent no taller than the sticky element itself.

Positioned elements can overlap; `z-index` decides which one is on top, covered in the stacking context lesson.
takeaways: absolute is relative to the nearest positioned ancestor
relative keeps the original space; absolute removes it
sticky needs an offset (top: 0) and breaks inside overflow ancestors
inset: 0 fills the containing block
pitfalls: A sticky header that never sticks because an ancestor has overflow: hidden.

quiz.q: An absolutely positioned child has top: 0; right: 0, but its parent is position: static. What is it positioned against?
options: The viewport, and it stays fixed while scrolling
The nearest ancestor with non-static position, or the initial containing block
quiz.explain: Only positioned ancestors form a containing block for absolute positioning.

concepts.name: CSS Grid
concepts.summary: Build two-dimensional layouts with grid-template-columns, fr units, repeat, minmax, auto-fit and named areas.
concepts.why: Grid turns page layouts, galleries and dashboards that used to need hacks or ready-made layout kits into a few lines of CSS.
concepts.body:
`display: grid` lays children out in rows and columns at once.

**Defining tracks**: each row or column of a grid is a **track**. `grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr 1fr` makes three columns. The `fr` unit takes a share of the leftover space: here the two `1fr` columns split it equally. `repeat(3, 1fr)` is three equal columns, and `minmax(200px, 1fr)` is a track that's at least 200px and grows to share space. Rows are created automatically as needed; `grid-auto-rows` sizes them. `gap` spaces rows and columns.

A gallery that adapts to any screen width takes one line, with no media queries (rules for particular screen sizes, from their own lesson): `grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(220px, 1fr))` fits as many 220px+ columns as there's room for, and stretches them to fill the row.

**Placing items**: by default items fill cells in order. To place one yourself, use the numbered lines between tracks: `grid-column: 1 / 3` spans from line 1 to line 3, or `grid-column: span 2`. Negative numbers count from the end, so `1 / -1` spans the full width.

**Named areas** make page layouts readable:

```css
grid-template-areas: "head head" "side main" "foot foot";
```

then `grid-area: main` on a child. Each quoted line is one row of the map. Changing the map for wider screens rearranges the whole layout.

Alignment works like flexbox: `justify-items`/`align-items` within cells, and `place-items: center` for both. Choose grid when you think in rows *and* columns, flexbox when content in one line should decide its own size.
takeaways: fr shares the leftover space; minmax() sets a range
repeat(auto-fit, minmax(X, 1fr)) is a responsive grid with no media queries
grid-column: 1 / -1 spans the full width
Named areas make layouts readable and easy to rearrange
pitfalls: Using grid-column: 1 / 3 and expecting it to span three columns; it spans lines 1 to 3, two columns.

quiz.q: grid-template-columns: 100px 1fr 2fr in a 400px wide container with no gap. How wide is the last column?
quiz.explain: 300px is free after the fixed column; 2fr of 3fr total is 200px.

concepts.name: Sizing, overflow and aspect ratio
concepts.summary: Control box sizes with min/max limits, min(), max(), clamp(), aspect-ratio and object-fit, and handle content that overflows.
concepts.why: Real content is unpredictable; limits instead of fixed sizes keep layouts intact with long words and odd images.
concepts.body: Fixed `width` and `height` break as soon as the content changes. Set limits instead: - `max-width: 100%` stops images growing wider than their parent; `min-height` lets a box grow with its content instead of clipping it. - `width: min(100%, 60rem)` picks the smaller of two values, a one-line way to make a column that never gets too wide. `max()` picks the larger; `clamp(min, preferred, max)` combines both. - `aspect-ratio: 16 / 9` gives a box a ratio, with the height computed from the width. Great for video embeds and card images. - `object-fit: cover` makes an `` fill its box, cropping instead of stretching; `object-position` picks the focal point. When content is bigger than its box, `overflow` decides what happens: `visible` (default, spills out), `hidden` (clipped), `auto` (scrollbars only when needed), `scroll` (always) and `clip` (like hidden, but the box can't be scrolled even by code). `overflow-x` and `overflow-y` set each axis. Long unbroken text, like a URL, spills out of narrow boxes. `overflow-wrap: anywhere` lets them break. For a single line with an ellipsis, combine `white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis`. For several lines, use `line-clamp`, written today with the old browser-specific prefix: `-webkit-line-clamp` together with `display: -webkit-box` and `-webkit-box-orient: vertical`. `scrollbar-gutter: stable` reserves space for a scrollbar so content doesn't shift when one appears.
takeaways: Prefer min/max limits to fixed sizes
min(), max() and clamp() compute responsive sizes
aspect-ratio + object-fit: cover for consistent media boxes
text-overflow: ellipsis needs nowrap and overflow: hidden
pitfalls: Setting a fixed height on a text container, which clips or overflows when the text grows.

quiz.q: What does width: min(100%, 600px) produce on a 400px-wide container?
quiz.explain: min() picks the smaller value: 100% of 400px is 400px.

concepts.name: Custom properties (CSS variables)
concepts.summary: Define reusable values with --name and read them with var(), with cascading, inheritance and fallbacks, to build themes.
concepts.why: Named, reusable values make consistent colours and spacing, themes and dark mode a matter of changing a few values.
concepts.body:
A **custom property**, often called a CSS **variable**, is a named value you can reuse. Its name starts with `--`. You set it like any declaration and read it with `var()`:

```css
:root { --brand: #4f46e5; }
.button { background: var(--brand); }
```

Some tools, such as Sass, offer variables that are swapped for their values before the browser sees the CSS. Custom properties are different: they live in the browser, take part in the cascade and inherit. Setting `--brand` on `:root` makes it available everywhere; setting it again on `.danger-zone` changes it for that element and everything inside it. Change one with JavaScript (`el.style.setProperty("--x", "10px")`) and everything using it updates at once.

`var(--gap, 1rem)` supplies a fallback used when the variable isn't defined. Fallbacks can nest: `var(--a, var(--b, 4px))`.

The browser stores a custom property's value as plain text and checks it only where it's used. If `--size: red` is used in `width: var(--size)`, the declaration is **invalid at computed-value time**: it's too late to drop it, so the property falls back to its inherited or initial value, not to an earlier declaration in your stylesheet.

Custom properties work well as **design tokens**: the named, agreed values of a design, such as its colours, spacing steps, corner radii and fonts. A theme, such as dark mode, then just sets those design tokens to new values:

- inside `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { ... }`, a block that applies only when the reader's device is set to dark mode (the media queries lesson covers these),
- or under a `[data-theme="dark"]` attribute that JavaScript switches on and off.

Custom properties can't be used in selectors or in `@media` conditions. To animate one, or to make the browser insist on a certain kind of value (a length, a colour), register it with `@property`.
takeaways: --name defines, var(--name, fallback) reads
Custom properties cascade and inherit, so they can be scoped
Theming = setting the design tokens again under @media or an attribute
Invalid values at use time fall back to inherited/initial, not earlier rules
pitfalls: Expecting var() to work inside a media query condition like @media (min-width: var(--bp)).

quiz.q: --pad is set to 8px on :root and 20px on .card. What padding does a .card .title with padding: var(--pad) get?
quiz.explain: Custom properties inherit, so the title sees the nearest definition: .card's 20px.

concepts.name: Media queries and responsive design
concepts.summary: Adapt layouts to screen size and user preferences with mobile-first media queries and checks of the reader's settings.
concepts.why: Most visits come from phones; responsive CSS is how one set of files serves every screen.
concepts.body:
**Responsive design** means one page that adapts to any screen. It rests on three things: the viewport meta tag in the HTML, flexible layouts (flexbox, grid, percentages), and **media queries** for the changes flexibility can't handle.

A media query applies rules only when a condition is true:

```css
@media (width >= 48rem) { .nav { display: flex; } }
```

Comparisons like `width >= 48rem` or `30rem <= width < 60rem` work in all current browsers. They're clearer than the older `min-width`/`max-width` form, which means the same thing.

Write **mobile-first**: base styles for small screens, then `width >=` queries that add complexity as space grows. Small screens get the simplest CSS, and the cascade stays easy to follow. The widths where your layout changes are called **breakpoints**. Choose them where *your content* starts to look wrong, not by phone models. Using `em`/`rem` in queries makes them respect user font-size settings.

Media queries can also check the **reader's settings and device**:

- `prefers-color-scheme: dark` for dark mode,
- `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` to tone down animation, which matters for people who get dizzy or sick from on-screen motion,
- `hover: hover` and `pointer: coarse` to tell mouse users from touch users,
- `print` for print stylesheets.

Many layouts need fewer queries than you'd think: grid's `repeat(auto-fit, minmax())`, `flex-wrap` and `clamp()` adapt smoothly to any width. Use media queries for structural changes, like turning a stacked menu into a horizontal bar.
takeaways: Mobile-first: base styles small, add with width >= queries
Pick breakpoints where the content breaks
Respect prefers-reduced-motion and prefers-color-scheme
Flexible layouts reduce the number of queries you need
pitfalls: Desktop-first max-width queries whose rules keep undoing each other.

quiz.q: With mobile-first CSS, where do the styles for the smallest screens go?
options: Outside any media query, as the base styles
In a separate stylesheet loaded by JavaScript
quiz.explain: Mobile-first means the unconditional base is the small-screen layout, with width >= queries adding to it.

concepts.name: Transitions and keyframe animations
concepts.summary: Animate changes between states with transition, and run multi-step animations with @keyframes and the animation property.
concepts.why: Small, purposeful motion makes pages feel responsive and shows users what changed.
concepts.body:
**Transitions** animate a property from its old value to its new one when it changes, for example on `:hover` or when a class is toggled:

```css
.button { transition: background-color 150ms ease, transform 150ms ease; }
```

Each entry has a property, a duration, an optional **timing function** and a delay. The timing function shapes the speed over time: `linear` is steady, `ease` starts slow, speeds up and slows down at the end; `ease-in-out`, `cubic-bezier()` and `steps()` give other curves. List specific properties rather than `transition: all`, which animates things you didn't intend and makes the browser do extra work.

Not everything can transition. Properties with no in-between values, like `display`, used to just flip. Now `transition-behavior: allow-discrete` together with `@starting-style`, which sets the "before" look of an element that has just appeared, lets pop-up panels such as dialogs fade in and out.

**Keyframe animations** run on their own, without a state change:

```css
@keyframes spin { to { rotate: 1turn; } }
.loader { animation: spin 1s linear infinite; }
```

The `animation` property sets the name, duration, timing function, delay, how many times it repeats (`infinite` for ever), direction (`alternate` plays back and forth) and `fill-mode` (`forwards` keeps the final look).

Smooth motion means drawing about 60 pictures, or **frames**, per second. Animate `transform` and `opacity` where you can: the browser can move or fade an already-drawn picture of the element without working out the page's layout again. Animating `width`, `top` or `margin` makes it recalculate the size and position of boxes on every frame, which can stutter.

Always respect `prefers-reduced-motion`, the reader's setting asking for less motion: replace large movements with fades or nothing.
takeaways: transition animates between states; @keyframes runs a sequence
List specific properties, not transition: all
Animate transform/translate and opacity for smooth motion
@starting-style animates elements as they appear
pitfalls: Animating height or top, which makes the browser redo the layout on every frame.

quiz.q: Which property change is cheapest for the browser to animate?
quiz.explain: The browser can move an already-drawn picture of the element without redoing layout or repainting it.

concepts.name: Transforms
concepts.summary: Move, rotate, scale and skew elements visually with transform and the individual translate, rotate and scale properties.
concepts.why: Transforms power hover effects, icons, carousels and smooth animations without disturbing the layout.
concepts.body:
Transforms change how an element is drawn without changing layout: its original box still occupies the same space, and neighbours don't move.

A transform is written as one or more functions:

- `translate(x, y)` moves it; percentages are relative to the element's own size, so `translate(-50%, -50%)` shifts by half its own width and height.
- `rotate(45deg)` (or `0.25turn`), `scale(1.1)` or `scale(x, y)`, `skew(10deg)`.
- 3D: `rotateY()`, `translateZ()`, `perspective()`.

When you list several functions in `transform`, **order matters**, because each one works in the space the previous ones have already moved and turned: `rotate(45deg) translateX(100px)` moves along the rotated axis, while `translateX(100px) rotate(45deg)` moves right and then rotates in place.

Modern CSS also has the individual properties `translate`, `rotate` and `scale`. They're applied in a fixed order (translate, rotate, scale, then `transform`), and you can change one without repeating the others, which is ideal for transitions and hover states.

`transform-origin` sets the pivot point; the default is the center. `transform-origin: top left` makes a menu grow out from its corner.

Two surprises: a transform creates a new **stacking context** (a separate layering group, explained in the z-index lesson), and it becomes the containing block for `position: fixed` descendants, so a fixed element inside a transformed parent stops staying put when the page scrolls.
takeaways: Transforms don't affect layout; neighbours stay put
Function order in transform matters
translate, rotate and scale properties can be changed independently
A transform creates a stacking context and traps fixed descendants inside it
pitfalls: Putting a position: fixed modal inside a transformed parent and seeing it scroll with the page.

quiz.q: A box is translated 50px to the right with transform. What happens to the element after it?
options: It moves into the gap left behind
It stays where it was; layout is unchanged
It wraps to the next line
quiz.explain: Transforms are purely visual; the original box keeps its place in layout.

concepts.name: :is(), :where() and :has()
concepts.summary: Group selectors with :is() and :where() (which has zero specificity), and select an element by what it contains with :has().
concepts.why: :has() finally lets CSS style an element based on what it contains, replacing a lot of JavaScript that adds and removes classes.
concepts.body:
Three pseudo-classes that take a list of selectors in brackets changed how CSS is written.

**:is()** takes a selector list and matches any of them: `:is(h1, h2, h3) a` instead of three selectors. Its specificity is that of the **most specific** selector inside it, so `:is(#id, p)` counts as an id everywhere.

**:where()** works the same way but always has **zero specificity**. It's perfect for default styles that any other rule should easily beat: `:where(ul, ol)[role="list"] { list-style: none; }`.

**:has()** selects an element by what's around it. `A:has(B)` matches A if a B can be found starting from A:

- `.card:has(img)` is a card that contains an image (a "parent selector").
- `h2:has(+ p)` is an h2 immediately followed by a p (looking ahead at its siblings).
- `form:has(:user-invalid)` is a form with an invalid field, to dim its send button.
- `body:has(dialog[open])` stops the page scrolling while a pop-up dialog is open.
- `label:has(input:checked)` styles the label of a checked input.

`:has()` takes the specificity of the most specific selector inside it, like `:is()`, and it can't be nested inside another `:has()`.

Browsers optimise these well, but avoid extremely broad selectors like `*:has(*)` on very large pages. With `:has()`, `:is()` and `:where()`, many state classes that JavaScript used to toggle become plain CSS.
takeaways: :is() groups selectors and takes the highest specificity of the selectors inside it
:where() groups with zero specificity
:has() selects an element by its descendants or following siblings
pitfalls: Putting an id inside :is() and accidentally raising the specificity of the whole selector.

quiz.q: What is the specificity of :where(#main .nav) a?
quiz.explain: :where() contributes zero, leaving only the type selector a.

concepts.name: Native CSS nesting
concepts.summary: Write nested rules directly in CSS with & and nested at-rules, without extra tools like Sass.
concepts.why: Nesting keeps component styles together and removes the main reason many projects used Sass, a tool that turns an extended CSS language into plain CSS.
concepts.body:
Every current browser understands nesting directly. Inside a rule you can write further rules that apply relative to the parent selector.

```css
.card {
  padding: 1rem;
  & h2 { margin: 0; }          /* .card h2 */
  &:hover { background: #f8f8f8; }  /* .card:hover */
  .dark & { background: #222; }    /* .dark .card */
}
```

`&` stands for the parent selector. A nested selector without `&` is treated as a descendant, so `h2 { }` inside `.card` means `.card h2` (the `&` is optional there). Use `&` explicitly when attaching pseudo-classes (`&:hover`) or when the parent goes in the middle or end (`.dark &`).

At-rules such as `@media` (rules for certain screen sizes), `@container`, `@supports` and `@layer` can sit inside a rule and apply to its selector. That keeps the changes for other screen sizes right next to the styles they change.

Differences from Sass to know:

- No gluing text onto names: `&__title` (a naming style from the architecture lesson) does **not** become `.card__title`.
- `&` stands for the whole parent selector list as one unit. If the parent is `#a, .b`, nested rules count with the id's specificity, even where they match `.b` elements.
- Declarations written after nested rules are allowed; they're treated as if in their original order.

Don't nest deeply. Each level adds specificity and ties your styles to the exact HTML structure; one or two levels is plenty.
takeaways: & is the parent selector; nested selectors default to descendants
Media and container queries can nest inside rules
No Sass-style gluing of names like &__title
Keep nesting to one or two levels
pitfalls: Copying Sass code that builds class names like &__title and getting silently broken selectors.

quiz.q: Inside .btn { ... }, what does '&.primary' select?
quiz.explain: With no space, & joins the selectors on the same element.

concepts.name: Container queries
concepts.summary: Make components respond to the size of their container rather than the viewport with container-type and @container.
concepts.why: A card that adapts to its slot works in a sidebar, a grid or full width without page-level breakpoints.
concepts.body:
Media queries ask about the viewport, but a component doesn't know where it will be placed: the same card may sit in a narrow sidebar or a wide main column. **Container queries** let it respond to the space it actually has.

Two steps:

- Mark an ancestor as a container: `container-type: inline-size`. Inline size means the width, for text written across the page. Optionally name it with `container-name: sidebar`, or use the shorthand `container: sidebar / inline-size`.
- Query it: `@container (width >= 30rem) { ... }`. Rules inside apply to descendants of the nearest container that matches (or the named one: `@container sidebar (width >= 30rem)`).

A container can't style itself based on its own size; queries apply to its descendants. In return, the container's width must not depend on its children. That's normal for blocks and grid cells, but not for elements that shrink to fit their content. Use `container-type: size` only if you also need to query height, because then the container needs a height set explicitly.

**Container query units** size things relative to the container: `cqi` is 1% of its inline size, so `font-size: clamp(1rem, 4cqi, 2rem)` gives type that scales with the card.

**Style queries** like `@container style(--variant: compact)` check the value of a custom property (CSS variable) on the container. Chrome, Edge and Safari support them; check before relying on them.

Use media queries for page-level layout and container queries for reusable components.
takeaways: container-type: inline-size makes an element queryable
@container rules apply to descendants, never the container itself
cqi units size relative to the container
Media queries for pages, container queries for components
pitfalls: Querying an element's own size; the query must target an ancestor container.

quiz.q: Why can't an element with container-type: inline-size use @container to change its own width?
options: Queries apply to descendants; restyling the container could create a loop
quiz.explain: Size containment requires the container's size not to depend on what the query changes.

concepts.name: Cascade layers
concepts.summary: Organise styles into @layer groups so whole layers win or lose regardless of specificity, taming resets, other people's CSS and small helper classes.
concepts.why: Layers end specificity fights between your own CSS and CSS written by someone else.
concepts.body:
**Cascade layers** add a step to the cascade that's checked *before* specificity. Declare the order once:

```css
@layer reset, base, components, utilities;
```

Then put rules into layers with `@layer components { ... }`, or with `@import url(lib.css) layer(vendor)`, which pulls in another CSS file as a layer. A declaration in a later layer beats one in an earlier layer, **however specific** the earlier selector is. So `.mt-0` in `utilities` beats `#sidebar .card h2` in `components`.

Rules:

- Unlayered styles beat all layered styles (for normal declarations). Put CSS you didn't write, such as a downloaded date picker's styles, in an early layer and it can never accidentally beat yours.
- Order is set by the first time a layer name appears, so declare the full order at the very top.
- Layers can nest (`@layer components.buttons`).
- `!important` reverses the order: an important declaration in an *earlier* layer beats one in a later layer, and important layered styles beat important unlayered ones. That lets a reset layer protect values that must never change.

Within a layer the normal rules still apply: specificity, then source order.

The `revert-layer` value rolls a property back to what the previous layers would have given it.

Layers suit a **design system** (a team's shared set of styles and components) well: resets lowest, then base styles for plain elements, then components, and **utility classes** on top. Utility classes are tiny classes that do one thing, like `.mb-0` for `margin-bottom: 0`, and on top they always win without `!important`. The Tailwind CSS framework (version 4) is built exactly this way.
takeaways: Layer order is checked before specificity
Declare the order up front: @layer a, b, c;
Unlayered styles beat layered ones
!important reverses layer order
pitfalls: Leaving most CSS unlayered and then wondering why layered framework styles never win.

quiz.q: A rule in @layer base uses #id .a (high specificity); a rule in a later layer uses .a. Which wins?
options: The base rule, because of the id
Whichever comes last in the file
Neither; they conflict and both are dropped
quiz.explain: Layer order is compared before specificity, so the later layer wins.

concepts.name: z-index and stacking contexts
concepts.summary: Understand painting order, z-index and the stacking contexts that make a z-index: 9999 still appear behind something.
concepts.why: Overlapping menus, modals and tooltips fail in confusing ways until stacking contexts make sense.
concepts.body:
When boxes overlap, the browser paints (draws) them in a fixed order. `z-index` changes that order, but only within a **stacking context**.

`z-index` works on positioned elements (any position except static) and on flex and grid items. Higher values paint on top of lower ones *in the same stacking context*.

A **stacking context** is a group that is painted as a unit: its children are layered among themselves, then the whole group is placed in its parent context according to its own z-index. A child can never escape its context. A modal with `z-index: 9999` inside a parent context at `z-index: 1` still sits below a sibling context at `z-index: 2`.

Many properties create a new stacking context, often unintentionally:

- `position` relative/absolute with a `z-index` other than auto; `position: fixed` or `sticky` always,
- `opacity` below 1, `transform`, `filter`, and blending effects such as `backdrop-filter` and `mix-blend-mode`,
- `isolation: isolate`, `will-change` and `contain: paint` (performance hints from the Expert level), and `container-type` from container queries.

To find the problem: look for the nearest ancestors that form stacking contexts and compare *their* z-index values, not the child's.

Good practice: keep a small, fixed scale of z-index values in custom properties (dropdown 10, sticky 20, modal 30); put `isolation: isolate` on components to keep their internal z-indexes inside; and for pop-ups use the HTML `dialog` element and `popover` attribute, which the browser draws in the **top layer**, a special layer above every stacking context.
takeaways: z-index only compares elements within the same stacking context
opacity < 1, transform, filter and more create contexts
Fix layering by adjusting the ancestor context
dialog and popover use the top layer, above everything
pitfalls: Escalating z-index values on a child whose ancestor context is the real problem.

quiz.q: A tooltip has z-index: 1000 but appears under a sibling section. Its parent has opacity: 0.99. Why?
options: The parent forms a stacking context, so the tooltip's z-index only applies inside it
quiz.explain: opacity below 1 creates a stacking context that contains the tooltip.

concepts.name: Organising CSS at scale
concepts.summary: Keep large stylesheets maintainable with naming rules like BEM, styles limited to one component, @scope, design tokens and utility classes.
concepts.why: CSS is global by default; without structure, every change risks breaking a distant page.
concepts.body:
Every CSS rule is global, so large projects need conventions to stay maintainable. The approaches overlap, and most modern projects mix them.

**Naming conventions.** BEM names classes as block, element and modifier: `.card`, `.card__title`, `.card--featured`. Every selector is a single class, so specificity stays flat, and the names show where a style belongs.

**Scoping** means making styles apply to one component only. Build tools such as CSS Modules, and JavaScript frameworks such as Vue, Svelte and Angular, rename your classes so each component's are unique. Web components (custom HTML elements built with JavaScript) can keep their styles in a hidden, separate part of the page called the shadow DOM.

CSS itself now has `@scope (.card) to (.card__content) { ... }`: the rules apply only inside `.card`, and stop at `.card__content`. When two scopes compete, **scoping proximity** makes the nearer one win.

**Utility-first.** Frameworks like Tailwind put many small utility classes straight into the HTML. That avoids inventing names and leaves no unused CSS behind, at the cost of long class lists.

**Design tokens.** Spacing, colour and type scales defined once as custom properties keep everything consistent and make theming possible.

**Layers.** `@layer reset, base, components, utilities` sets precedence explicitly.

General rules:

- Keep specificity low and flat: classes, not ids or long chains.
- Style components independently of where they appear; let parents handle layout (gap, grid) instead of children setting outer margins.
- Co-locate styles with components and delete them with the component.
- Check your CSS with a linter such as Stylelint, which flags mistakes and risky code, and let a formatter tidy the spacing automatically.
takeaways: Global CSS needs conventions: naming, scoping or utilities
Keep specificity flat with single-class selectors
Design tokens + layers give consistency and predictable precedence
@scope limits rules to one part of the page, with an inner boundary where they stop
pitfalls: Components that set their own outer margins, which breaks them in new contexts.

quiz.q: Why does BEM recommend .card__title over .card h2?
options: Single-class selectors keep specificity flat and don't depend on the exact HTML structure
h2 elements can't be styled with classes
quiz.explain: A unique class avoids specificity growth and survives changes like switching h2 to h3.

concepts.name: Formatting contexts and margin collapsing
concepts.summary: Learn how block and inline formatting contexts work, when margins collapse, and how display: flow-root keeps floated elements inside their parent.
concepts.why: Strange gaps, escaped margins and collapsed parents all follow from formatting-context rules.
concepts.body:
Layout in CSS is organised into **formatting contexts**: regions where boxes are laid out by one set of rules.

A **block formatting context** (BFC) stacks block boxes vertically. Inside one, vertical margins of adjacent blocks **collapse**: the gap is the larger of the two margins (or the sum of the largest positive and most negative). Collapse also happens between a parent and its first or last child when nothing separates them (no border, padding, inline content or height). That's why a child's `margin-top` can appear *outside* its parent, pushing the parent down.

A **float** (`float: left` or `right`) is an older feature: the box moves to one side and the following text wraps around it, like a photo in a magazine column. Floats were once used for whole page layouts, and they explain several BFC rules.

A new BFC is created by the `<html>` element, floats, absolutely positioned elements, inline-blocks, table cells, `overflow` other than visible/clip, flex and grid items, and explicitly by **`display: flow-root`**. Margins never collapse across a BFC boundary, and a BFC contains its floats: the classic fix for a parent with zero height because all children float is `display: flow-root`.

An **inline formatting context** lays out text and inline boxes in **line boxes**. Each line's height comes from `line-height` and the tallest inline content aligned by `vertical-align`. Images are inline by default and sit on the text baseline, leaving a small gap underneath for the parts of letters like g and y that hang below the line; `display: block` or `vertical-align: middle` removes it.

Flex and grid containers establish their own **flex/grid formatting contexts**, where margins never collapse and floats don't apply. This is one reason spacing with `gap` in flex or grid is more predictable than stacking margins.
takeaways: Vertical margins collapse inside a BFC, including parent/first-child
display: flow-root creates a BFC and changes nothing else
BFCs contain floats and block margin collapse across their edge
Flex and grid contexts never collapse margins
pitfalls: Adding padding: 1px hacks to stop margin collapse instead of display: flow-root.

quiz.q: A section with no padding or border contains an h1 with margin-top: 40px. Where does the gap appear?
options: Inside the section, above the h1
Nowhere; margins on headings are ignored
Above the section, because the margin collapses through
quiz.explain: With nothing separating them, the child's top margin collapses with the parent's and shows outside it.

concepts.name: The rendering pipeline and performance
concepts.summary: Follow how style, layout, paint and composite turn CSS into pixels, and use that to avoid stutter, layout thrashing and slow pages.
concepts.why: Smooth scrolling and animation depend on knowing which CSS changes are cheap and which redo the whole page.
concepts.body:
The browser reads the HTML into the **DOM**, its tree of the page's elements, and the CSS into the **CSSOM**, a matching model of all the style rules. It then turns the two into pixels in stages:

- **Style**: compute the final value of every property for every element (selector matching, cascade, inheritance).
- **Layout** (also called reflow): compute each box's size and position.
- **Paint**: record drawing commands for text, colours, borders and shadows, split into layers.
- **Composite**: the graphics chip (GPU) stacks the layers into the final frame.

A change only redoes the stages from where it enters. Changing `width`, `font-size` or `margin` triggers layout, paint and composite. Changing `color` or `background` skips layout. Changing `transform` or `opacity` on an element with its own layer can skip straight to composite, which is why animations should use them.

**Layout thrashing** happens when a script changes a style and then reads a size, such as `offsetHeight`, over and over. Each read forces the browser to redo layout on the spot, before it can answer. Do all the reads first and the writes after, or schedule the writes with `requestAnimationFrame`, which runs code just before the next frame is drawn.

Tools for containing the cost:

- `will-change: transform` hints that an element will animate so the browser can promote it to a layer ahead of time. Use it sparingly; every layer uses memory.
- `contain: layout paint` (or `content`) promises that nothing inside the element affects the layout outside it, limiting how much is redone.
- `content-visibility: auto` skips rendering off-screen sections entirely; pair it with `contain-intrinsic-size` to keep scrollbars stable.

Matching selectors is rarely what slows a page today; huge numbers of elements and forced layouts usually are. Measure with the Performance panel in developer tools, which colours style, layout, paint and composite work separately.
takeaways: Pipeline: style, layout, paint, composite
transform and opacity animations can skip layout and paint
Interleaving style writes and layout reads causes thrashing
content-visibility: auto skips off-screen rendering
pitfalls: Putting will-change on many elements permanently, wasting GPU memory.

quiz.q: Changing which property most likely triggers layout?
quiz.explain: Width changes geometry, so layout, paint and composite all run again.

concepts.name: Modern colour: oklch, color-mix, relative colour
concepts.summary: Use oklch, extra-vivid P3 colours, color-mix() and relative colours to build whole palettes in plain CSS.
concepts.why: Generating hover states, tints and themes from one brand colour removes hand-maintained colour tables.
concepts.body:
A **colour space** is a system for describing colours with numbers. Hex, `rgb()` and `hsl()` all describe the same one, **sRGB**, the standard range of colours screens have shown for decades. CSS now goes well beyond it.

**Colour spaces.** sRGB doesn't match how eyes see: `hsl(60 100% 50%)` yellow looks far lighter than `hsl(240 100% 50%)` blue at the same "lightness". `oklch(L C H)` and `oklab()` are **perceptually uniform**: equal L means equal perceived lightness, which makes accessible palettes and consistent contrast much easier. The **gamut** is the range of colours a screen can show. Many modern screens show more vivid colours than sRGB (a **wide gamut**), reached with `color(display-p3 1 0 0)` or oklch with a high chroma. A colour a screen can't show is replaced by the nearest one it can, so give an sRGB fallback where the exact colour matters.

**color-mix()** blends two colours in a chosen space: `color-mix(in oklch, var(--brand), white 20%)`. Mixing in oklab or oklch avoids the muddy grey midpoints of sRGB mixing.

**Relative colour syntax** derives a colour from another: `oklch(from var(--brand) calc(l - 0.1) c h)` is a darker brand for hover, and `rgb(from var(--brand) r g b / 50%)` adds transparency. One base colour generates a whole scale.

**light-dark()** picks a value by the element's `color-scheme`: `color: light-dark(#111, #eee)`, with `color-scheme: light dark` on `:root`.

The colour space used to work out in-between colours matters in gradients too: `linear-gradient(in oklch, blue, yellow)` avoids the grey middle that sRGB gradients produce.

Finally, check contrast: how much text stands out from its background. Even lightness helps, but the accessibility guidelines (WCAG) set minimum contrast ratios that you must still check with a tool.
takeaways: oklch is perceptually uniform: equal L looks equally light
color-mix(in oklch, ...) blends without muddy midpoints
Relative colour syntax derives hover and alpha variants from one base colour
light-dark() + color-scheme for simple theming
pitfalls: Assuming equal hsl lightness means equal perceived lightness or contrast.

quiz.q: What does oklch(from var(--c) l c calc(h + 180)) produce?
options: The complementary hue at the same lightness and chroma
quiz.explain: It keeps l and c and rotates the hue by 180 degrees.

concepts.name: Intrinsic sizing and the flex algorithm
concepts.summary: Master min-content, max-content and fit-content, how flex items grow and shrink, and why min-width: auto causes overflow.
concepts.why: Mysterious overflow in flex and grid layouts is almost always an intrinsic-size rule at work.
concepts.body:
Boxes have **intrinsic sizes** derived from their content:

- `min-content`: the narrowest the box can be without overflowing, roughly its longest word or widest image.
- `max-content`: its width if nothing wrapped.
- `fit-content`: max-content, but capped at the available space (and at least min-content).

These values work in `width`, `grid-template-columns` and elsewhere. `width: fit-content` shrink-wraps a block, and `grid-template-columns: max-content 1fr` sizes a label column to its longest label.

**How flex sizes items.** Each item starts at its `flex-basis` (or its width, or its content size when the basis is `auto`). The leftover space is then shared out in proportion to `flex-grow`; if the items are too big, the shortfall is taken away in proportion to `flex-shrink` × basis. That's why `flex: 1` (basis 0) gives equal columns while `flex: auto` (basis auto) gives columns proportional to their content.

**The automatic minimum.** Flex items have `min-width: auto` by default, which resolves to their min-content size. An item containing a long URL, a `<pre>` block or a wide table refuses to shrink below that and overflows the container. The fix is `min-width: 0` on the flex item (or `overflow: hidden`, which also sets the automatic minimum to 0). Grid has the same issue: `1fr` means `minmax(auto, 1fr)`, so use `minmax(0, 1fr)` for tracks that must be able to shrink.

Percentage heights only work when the parent has a definite height, one known without measuring the content; flex and grid stretching usually provide one, which is why `height: 100%` works in some layouts and not others.
takeaways: min-content, max-content and fit-content size boxes from their content
flex: 1 (basis 0) gives equal columns; flex: auto doesn't
Flex items default to min-width: auto; set min-width: 0 to let them shrink
Use minmax(0, 1fr) for grid tracks that must shrink
pitfalls: Fixing flex overflow by adding overflow: hidden on the container instead of min-width: 0 on the item.

quiz.q: A flex: 1 item contains a wide code block and overflows the row. What is the usual fix?
quiz.explain: The automatic minimum size keeps the item at its min-content width; min-width: 0 removes it.
